title: John
subtitle: the Word made flesh, so that you may believe
lead: The Gospel of John tells the story of Jesus from a height no other Gospel climbs. It opens before creation: "In the beginning was the Word" (1:1). Then it walks the roads of Galilee, Samaria and Judea with careful detail, from the stone water jars at Cana to the five porches at the pool of Bethesda. Jesus goes up to Jerusalem for the festivals, does seven "signs", speaks in long conversations and speeches, washes his disciples' feet, dies on the cross at Passover and rises to meet Mary Magdalene, Thomas and Peter.

The book says plainly why it was written: so that its readers would believe that Jesus is the Messiah, the Son of God, and by believing have life in his name (20:31). Church tradition names the writer John, the son of Zebedee, the "disciple Jesus loved". The Gospel itself names no author, and scholars still debate who wrote it, when, and for whom. Most date it to about AD 90–100. John has 21 chapters and 879 verses, and about nine tenths of it has no parallel in Matthew, Mark or Luke.
facts: Not named in the text. The book says it rests on the witness of "the disciple Jesus loved" (21:20–24). From about AD 180, Irenaeus and later writers name him John, the son of Zebedee, one of the Twelve. Others have proposed John the Elder, a disciple known to Papias; an unnamed Judean disciple; or a school of the disciple's followers who finished the book (see "Who wrote John?" below).

Most scholars: about AD 90–100. A minority argue for the 60s or earlier, before the Temple fell in AD 70 (J. A. T. Robinson). The papyrus fragment P52, with lines of John 18, has often been dated about AD 125–175, though Brent Nongbri and others allow the late 100s or early 200s; its exact date is debated.
Ephesus, by early tradition (Irenaeus). Some scholars suggest Syria, Alexandria, or the lands east of the Jordan.
The ministry of Jesus in Galilee, Samaria and above all Jerusalem, across about three Passovers (2:13; 6:4; 11:55), told, most scholars think, for readers after the Temple's fall.
A Gospel: an ancient life of Jesus built around seven signs, long conversations and speeches, a farewell discourse and a passion narrative. Many scholars compare it to ancient biographies (bioi).
Greek, simple in vocabulary and grammar but deep in meaning; it explains Hebrew and Aramaic words for its readers ("Rabbi", "Messiah", "Cephas", 1:38–42).

audience.to: The Gospel speaks to "you" (19:35; 20:31): readers who did not see Jesus but are told about him by a witness (20:29). It explains Jewish customs and words (2:6; 4:9; 19:40) and translates Aramaic, so many of its readers were not from Judea and did not know Aramaic. Yet it assumes they know the Jewish Scriptures, the festivals and figures like Moses, Abraham and Jacob. Most scholars think it was written for churches, perhaps around Ephesus, near the end of the first century, made up of Jews and non-Jews who believed in Jesus, at a time when believers in Jesus and the synagogue were drawing apart (9:22; 12:42; 16:2).
audience.why: The book states its own aim: that readers believe Jesus is the Messiah, the Son of God, and through believing have life in his name (20:31). It sets out signs and witnesses, from John the Baptist to Thomas, so that readers will trust Jesus as the one who comes from the Father and makes him known (1:18). For believers who had lost the Temple (if, as most think, it was written after AD 70), who felt pushed out of synagogue life (9:22; 16:2; how formal that was is debated) and who waited for the Lord, it shows Jesus as the true Temple, the true bread and the true light, and it promises the Advocate, the Spirit who keeps them in his word.
views: J. Louis Martyn and Raymond Brown read John on two levels: the story of Jesus and, beneath it, the story of a "Johannine community" that had been put out of its synagogue (9:22). On this view the harsh lines about "the Jews" reflect a painful family quarrel in the writer's own time. Martyn tied 9:22 to the Twelfth Benediction, a synagogue prayer against minim (heretics); Reuven Kimelman, Daniel Boyarin and Adele Reinhartz argue that the evidence does not support a formal expulsion of believers in John's day, so the conflict, if real, was local and informal.
Believers who need to keep believing

Many read 20:31 as written to strengthen Christians: the best manuscripts may read "so that you may go on believing" (Greek present tense). The farewell discourses (13–17) speak to disciples, not outsiders.

Others (W. C. van Unnik, J. A. T. Robinson, D. A. Carson) think John was written to win Jews and God-fearing Gentiles of the Greek-speaking Diaspora, following the other manuscript reading "so that you may come to believe."

Richard Bauckham and others argue that the Gospels were written for Christians everywhere, not for one small group, and that John expects readers who already know Mark's story (compare 3:24 and 11:2).

lenses.name: History and setting
lenses.desc: Reads John in its land and time: Jerusalem and its festivals, the Temple, Samaria and Mount Gerizim, Galilee, and John's exact places (Bethany beyond the Jordan, Jacob's well, Bethesda's five porches, the pool of Siloam). It weighs the historical value of John's own outline, with three Passovers and a crucifixion on the day the Passover lambs were slaughtered.

lenses.name: Critical
lenses.desc: Asks who the Beloved Disciple was and who finished the book; whether it grew in stages (a source of signs, a second edition, chapter 21 as an epilogue); what the "Johannine community" was; and how John relates to Matthew, Mark and Luke, whether it knew them or used separate traditions.

lenses.name: Literary
lenses.desc: Reads the finished Gospel as a crafted story: the prologue as an overture, signs that lead into long discourses, people who misunderstand Jesus and the irony the reader sees, the "I am" sayings, light and darkness, the "hour", and words with double meanings ("born from above", "lifted up").

lenses.name: Jewish reading
lenses.desc: Places John among Jewish texts and readers: the festivals as the setting of Jesus' words, Wisdom and the Word in Jewish thought, Moses and the Torah, and what "the Jews" means in John (all Jews, Judeans, or the Jerusalem leaders). It also faces how the Gospel was later used against Jews, with Jewish scholars such as Adele Reinhartz and Daniel Boyarin.

lenses.name: Church tradition
lenses.desc: How the churches have read John: Clement of Alexandria's "spiritual Gospel", the fathers' use of the prologue at Nicaea and Chalcedon to confess Christ as true God and true man, sacramental readings of water and Spirit (3:5), bread (6:53) and blood and water (19:34), and its place in worship, prayer and mission.

authorship: The book never names its author. At the end it says that the disciple Jesus loved, who leaned against Jesus at the last supper, "is the one giving testimony about these events, and the one who wrote them down", and a group adds, "we know his testimony is true" (21:20–24). So the Gospel presents itself as resting on an eyewitness, with others who vouch for him and probably finished the book. The Beloved Disciple appears only from chapter 13 on (13:23; 19:26–27, 35; 20:2–8; 21:7, 20), and perhaps as the unnamed disciple of 1:35–40 and 18:15.
Church tradition: John son of Zebedee

Irenaeus of Lyon, writing about AD 180, says "John, the disciple of the Lord, who also leaned on his breast, himself published a Gospel while living at Ephesus" (Against Heresies 3.1.1). He claimed to have learned this from Polycarp, who had known John. Polycrates of Ephesus (about 190) also says John who leaned on the Lord's breast was buried at Ephesus (in Eusebius, Church History 5.24.3), the Muratorian Fragment (probably late 100s) says John wrote at the urging of his fellow disciples, and Clement of Alexandria called John the "spiritual Gospel", written last after the others had set out the outward facts (in Eusebius 6.14.7). Many Catholic, Orthodox and evangelical scholars still hold that the apostle John, son of Zebedee, stands behind the book, pointing to its knowledge of Judea, Jerusalem and the temple, and to the fact that the apostle John is never named in it, as if the author kept himself out of view.

Papias, bishop of Hierapolis early in the 100s, lists among his sources both the apostle John and "John the Elder", a disciple of the Lord still living in his time (in Eusebius, Church History 3.39.4). Eusebius thought there were two Johns, and Martin Hengel and Richard Bauckham argue that the Elder, a Jerusalem disciple who was not one of the Twelve, was the Beloved Disciple and the author. This would explain the Gospel's focus on Judea and why the 2nd and 3rd Letters of John come from "the Elder".

Some have identified the Beloved Disciple with Lazarus, whom Jesus is said to love (11:3, 5, 36); with Thomas; with John Mark; or with an unnamed disciple from Jerusalem. Others think he is an ideal figure, the model disciple, rather than a person who can be identified.

Two late writers, Philip of Side (400s) and George the Sinner (800s), report that Papias said John son of Zebedee was killed by Jews, and Jesus' words to James and John about drinking his cup (Mark 10:39) have been read as a prophecy of martyrdom for both. Some critics use this to argue that the apostle died early and could not have written the Gospel late in the century. The reports are late, secondhand and possibly confused, so most scholars give them little weight.

Most critical scholars think the Gospel grew in stages. Rudolf Bultmann proposed a source of signs and a source of discourses; Raymond Brown described five stages, from an eyewitness's memories through preaching in a community to a final editor who added material such as chapter 21. Many hold that the Beloved Disciple was a real follower of Jesus, honored by the community, but that others wrote the Gospel in its present form. They point to differences from the other Gospels, the late-first-century conflict with the synagogue (9:22; 16:2), and the developed theology of the prologue.

A few Christians in Rome around 200 (Gaius and a group Epiphanius later called the Alogi) rejected John, even assigning it to the heretic Cerinthus, because its order of events differed from the other Gospels. The Gnostic teacher Heracleon wrote the first known commentary on it (about 170), and some scholars once thought John was mainly a Gnostic favorite, but Charles Hill and others have shown that it was widely used by mainstream Christians in the 100s too.

sections.h: When and where was John written?
sections.b:
Most scholars date John to about AD 90–100. They point to the expulsion of believers from synagogues (9:22; 12:42; 16:2), which they relate to growing separation after the temple's fall in AD 70, to the Gospel's developed theology, and to the tradition that John lived into the reign of Trajan (98–117). Some, such as John A. T. Robinson, date it before 70, noting that 5:2 says the pool of Bethesda "is" in Jerusalem and that the Gospel never mentions the temple's destruction.

A small papyrus scrap with lines of John 18:31–33 and 37–38, Papyrus 52 in Manchester, was once dated about AD 125 and used to rule out a late date. Brent Nongbri and others have argued that handwriting alone allows a date anywhere from about 125 to 175 or later. Papyrus 66 and Papyrus 75, nearly complete copies, date from around 200. Ephesus is the traditional place; others suggest Antioch in Syria, Alexandria, or (Klaus Wengst) the region east of the Jordan where Jewish authority was strong.

sections.h: John and the other three Gospels
sections.b:
About nine tenths of John has no parallel in Matthew, Mark and Luke. There are no parables in the usual sense, no exorcisms, no transfiguration and no institution of the Lord's Supper; instead there are long speeches and "I am" sayings. Jesus goes to Jerusalem for several festivals, so the ministry lasts two or three years, and the temple scene comes at the beginning (2:13–22). Jesus dies on the day of preparation for Passover, when the lambs were slaughtered (19:14), not after the Passover meal.

Did John know the other Gospels? Clement of Alexandria thought John wrote to supplement them. Percival Gardner-Smith (1938) argued that John wrote independently, from his own traditions, and C. H. Dodd showed how much old historical tradition John preserves. Since the 1970s many scholars (Frans Neirynck, Richard Bauckham) have argued that John knew Mark at least, and expected readers to know it (3:24; 11:2). Paul Anderson and others now take John's own details, such as the length of the ministry and the place names, as serious historical evidence, sometimes better than the Synoptics.

Parallel passages in John 1–4 include the Baptist's witness (1:19–34; Matthew 3; Mark 1:2–11), the call of Andrew and Peter (1:40–42; Matthew 4:18–22), the temple scene (2:13–22; Mark 11:15–17), the prophet without honor (4:44; Mark 6:4) and the official's son (4:46–54; Matthew 8:5–13).

John uses hoi Ioudaioi about seventy times, far more than the other Gospels. Sometimes it is neutral ("the Jews' Passover", 2:13), sometimes friendly ("salvation comes from the Jews", 4:22), and many Jews believe in Jesus (11:45). But often "the Jews" are Jesus' opponents, and in 8:44 Jesus tells a group of them that their father is the devil. Jesus, his mother, his disciples and the narrator are all Jews too.

Scholars explain the usage in several ways: "the Jews" often means the Jerusalem authorities; or "Judeans" in contrast to Galileans; or it reflects the bitter split between Jesus-believing Jews and synagogue leaders in John's own time. J. Louis Martyn linked the threat of being "thrown out of the synagogue" (9:22) to the Twelfth Benediction against minim, but Reuven Kimelman and Daniel Boyarin have shown that the prayer's date and target are uncertain, and many scholars now doubt any formal, widespread expulsion. Jewish scholars such as Adele Reinhartz argue that the Gospel invites readers to see "the Jews" as outsiders, whatever its original setting, and that this must be faced honestly. Christians later used verses like 8:44 to justify hatred of Jews. Since the Second Vatican Council (Nostra Aetate, 1965), the Catholic Church and many Protestant churches, among them the Evangelical Lutheran Church in America (1994), have rejected the charge that the Jews as a people are guilty of Jesus' death or rejected by God. This translation keeps "the Jews" where John says it, and the notes explain who is meant.

sections.h: "So that you may believe": the purpose of John
sections.b: John states his aim near the end: these signs "have been written down so that you may believe that Jesus is the Messiah, the Son of God, and so that as you believe, you will have life in his name" (20:31). The manuscripts differ on one letter. Some read pisteusēte (aorist: "come to believe"), others pisteuēte (present: "keep on believing"); the second is in the oldest copies of Sinaiticus and Vaticanus and probably Papyrus 66. The first suggests a book to win new believers; the second, a book to strengthen believers. Many scholars think the grammar cannot settle the question, and that the Gospel serves both purposes.

spec.title: Claude's theory: a Gospel built for rereading
spec.body: This is my own way of putting a point many scholars make in parts. John seems written to be read twice. On a first reading the reader follows characters who misunderstand Jesus: Nicodemus, the Samaritan woman, the crowds. On a second reading, knowing the end, the reader catches the double meanings ("lifted up", "born from above", "the hour", "destroy this temple") that the narrator only half explains (2:22; 12:16). The disciples themselves are said to understand only after the resurrection. If so, the Gospel's purpose in 20:31 fits both readings of the variant: the first time through it calls readers to believe; every later time it deepens a faith they already have.

prompts: An abstract scene before dawn over the hills of Judea: deep darkness above, a single line of pale gold light breaking along the horizon and spreading upward, no human figures, ancient rough terrain in the foreground, soft mist in the valleys, painterly realism, quiet and vast.

Inside the courtyard of a small stone house in a first-century Galilean village at a wedding: six large gray limestone jars, each knee to waist high with rounded bodies and thick rims, standing in a row; two servants in plain tunics dipping a cup into one jar; behind them guests at low tables under oil lamps and woven awnings; warm evening light.

A flat rooftop in Jerusalem at night under stars and a half moon: a bearded man in his forties in a plain cloak sits on a low stone ledge talking with an older, well-dressed Pharisee with a fringed prayer shawl over his shoulders; one oil lamp between them; the dark shapes of houses and the distant temple walls behind.

Midday in the hill country of Samaria: a low stone well rim in open ground with Mount Gerizim rising behind; a tired Galilean man in a dusty tunic sitting on the rim; a Samaritan woman in a long dark dress and head covering holding a clay water jar on her hip and a rope; bright overhead sun with short shadows; olive trees and terraced fields.

The classic Catholic commentary, careful on history, text and theology.

A clear evangelical commentary that defends traditional authorship.

A critical commentary that reads John as a trial of Jesus.

Argues that the Beloved Disciple was John the Elder, an eyewitness.

The pioneering literary study of John as a story.

A Jewish scholar on how John shapes readers' views of "the Jews".

The influential "two-level" reading of John 9 and the Johannine community.
